questions.stimulus:
I. Logitech CEO Hanneke Faber has set the AI cat among boardroom pigeons. She says she'd
welcome a bot member in every board meeting to stay ahead in the productivity curve. AI
agents are embedding themselves across business functions, and it is a matter of time before
they show up on company boards with their unbeatable data-driven analytical capabilities.
Bots have access to real-time business processes on a scale impossible to reach by humans.
Board decisions made on inputs by AI agents will be vastly superior, as will their execution
through digital agents. Faber is correct. Bring AI on board - but do it with circumspection.
Boardrooms exist not only to maximise corporate profits but also to ensure they are made
ethically. Corporate governance will have to remain entirely in the domain of humans given
AI's shortcomings. Culture and emotions drive corporate growth alongside business strategy.
The middle ground would be for boardrooms to power themselves up through AI bots and
then turn the decision-making over to directors for the human touch. Conflict resolution
between digital and human inputs would necessarily have to be guided by value judgement.
Boardrooms by design are good at asking ethical questions. They would get better at it if the
questions became granular through the introduction of AI-driven business strategies.
Corporate boards that use augmented intelligence are likely to improve productivity without
losing agency over governance. The composition of future boardrooms will be vital to
achieving the right balance between artificial and natural intelligence. Boards guide corporate
engagement with the external environment, and the pace of incorporating AI-driven decisions
will be influenced by technology dispersal. Business, however, is expected to push societal
adoption of AI and will have to work out the place for bots in decision-making. Humans will
have to be in the loop at almost every stage of AI implementation to be able to retain context
for intervention. Behind every R2D2, there must be a Luke Skywalker.
SOURCE:https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/opinion/et-editorial/bot-in-boardrooms-get-
ai-incorporated/articleshow/124641380.cms?from=mdr

questions.stimulus:
II. Stodgy textbooks tell you that collective bargaining began with the industrial revolution
and workers seeking to protect themselves against exploitation. You have updated the concept
as more jobs now come from outside factories, mills and mines. But it’s still associated with
the grim fight for minimum pay, accident insurance, transparency in algorithms…So you
might be shook that JITO, an Ahmedabad-based group of Jain industrialists, businessmen and
professionals, has used collective bargaining to get themselves Audis, BMWs, Mercs…They
jiffed top luxury brands into giving them a Rs 21cr discount.
Actually, the Richie Rich are not new to this romp at all. Different Indian mercantile
communities historically grew by negotiating with the colonialists as a coordinated bloc. In
the West, families like the Rothschilds and Agnellis grew into their extraordinary wealth and
power through mobilising oversized leverage. Family controlled conglomerates from Japan’s
Mitsubishi and Mitsui to South Korea’s Samsung and LG have done the same to get
favourable industrial policies and trade protections. BTW, what do you think oil barons of
Opec do? The Silicon Valley bros may compete aggressively with each other but they also
often act collectively, as when lobbying against proposed antitrust or privacy laws. So, if in
your head, it’s workers, wage earners, gig hands alone who are acting as a class, maybe have
a rethink.
If we book a bunch of hotel rooms for a family function, we demand a discount. If the real
moneybags buy some prime real estate in London or Mumbai, they do the same. Same
difference. The Rolex, Hermès and Ferraris also line up to do the tiptop for them. Jets, yachts,
vineyards, yes, they negotiate great prices for all these. Because they can. Not everyone
tattles like JITO though. Most golden bargains stay behind gilded curtains.
SOURCE: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/blogs/toi-editorials/luxediscount/

III. Days after brokering a fragile ceasefire in West Asia, US President Donald Trump has
turned his attention once again to Eastern Europe. His stance on the ongoing three-and-a-half-
year war has swung like a pendulum. In February, the Oval Office spat with Ukrainian
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was followed by threats of sanctions against Moscow. Then
at the Alaska Summit in August, Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin and appeared
to align himself with the Kremlin’s position — particularly Putin’s demand that Ukraine cede
unoccupied parts of the Donbas region in exchange for a ceasefire. Subsequently, Trump
threw his weight behind Kyiv and speculated in September that Ukraine could take back all
of its territory and “maybe even go further than that”. He even expressed openness to the idea
of supplying Tomahawk cruise missiles to Ukraine. Now, there is yet another reversal.
Following a lengthy call with Putin last week and a meeting with Zelenskyy on Friday,
Trump has urged Kyiv and Moscow to “stop where they are”, suggested that the war should
end by allowing the Donbas region to “be cut the way it is” (leaving most of it under Russian
control), and rejected Zelenskyy’s request for the Tomahawks.


Trump’s inconsistency is all too familiar and yet disquieting, not just for Ukraine, but also for
Europe. Over the past six weeks, Russia has sent drones over Poland and Romania, flown
fighter jets into Estonian airspace, and is accused of orchestrating drone flights that disrupted
airports in Denmark, Belgium, and Germany — allegations Moscow has denied. At the time,
Trump expressed clear solidarity with NATO, declaring that it should shoot down Russian
aircraft violating its airspace. Now, as the US president again presses Ukraine to make
concessions, it will be up to Europe to ensure that, in the event of a deal, robust security
assurances are provided to Ukraine.
An erratic Trump and an emboldened Putin illustrate the challenges that lie ahead in ending
the war. Trump has reportedly agreed to hold another summit in Hungary — an EU member
that opposes Ukraine’s accession and is led by the pro-Putin Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
Once again, it appears that Ukraine and Europe are being sidelined, with Washington
positioning itself as the arbiter of war and peace. If this trend continues, and given the US
president’s current stance, the day may not be far when Ukraine is left with little choice but to
yield to Trump’s terms and compromise on its territory. To avert that scenario, Europe will
need to act quickly.

turned his attention once again to Eastern Europe. His stance on the ongoing three-and-a-half-
year war has swung like a pendulum. In February, the Oval Office spat with Ukrainian
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was followed by threats of sanctions against Moscow. Then
at the Alaska Summit in August, Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin and appeared
to align himself with the Kremlin’s position — particularly Putin’s demand that Ukraine cede
unoccupied parts of the Donbas region in exchange for a ceasefire. Subsequently, Trump
threw his weight behind Kyiv and speculated in September that Ukraine could take back all
of its territory and “maybe even go further than that”. He even expressed openness to the idea
of supplying Tomahawk cruise missiles to Ukraine. Now, there is yet another reversal.
Following a lengthy call with Putin last week and a meeting with Zelenskyy on Friday,
Trump has urged Kyiv and Moscow to “stop where they are”, suggested that the war should
end by allowing the Donbas region to “be cut the way it is” (leaving most of it under Russian
control), and rejected Zelenskyy’s request for the Tomahawks.

Europe. Over the past six weeks, Russia has sent drones over Poland and Romania, flown
fighter jets into Estonian airspace, and is accused of orchestrating drone flights that disrupted
airports in Denmark, Belgium, and Germany — allegations Moscow has denied. At the time,
Trump expressed clear solidarity with NATO, declaring that it should shoot down Russian
aircraft violating its airspace. Now, as the US president again presses Ukraine to make
concessions, it will be up to Europe to ensure that, in the event of a deal, robust security
assurances are provided to Ukraine.

positioning itself as the arbiter of war and peace. If this trend continues, and given the US
president’s current stance, the day may not be far when Ukraine is left with little choice but to
yield to Trump’s terms and compromise on its territory. To avert that scenario, Europe will
need to act quickly.

questions.stimulus:
IV. India is quietly approaching a demographic turning point that its political vocabulary has
yet to fully acknowledge. While public debate remains dominated by growth rates,
employment numbers, and infrastructure expansion, a far slower transformation is unfolding
beneath the surface ~ the steady ageing of the population, often in isolation and uncertainty.
For decades, Indian society relied on the family as the primary institution of elder care. That
assumption is now fraying. Urban migration, smaller households, longer life expectancy, and
changing social norms have altered how ageing is experienced.
A growing number of older Indians are living alone or with equally frail spouses, navigating
declining health with limited daily support. What was once absorbed privately within
households is increasingly becoming a public challenge. The consequences are not merely
emotional. Ageing brings predictable medical and functional needs ~ mobility assistance,
chronic disease management, memory care, and companionship. Yet India’s health system
remains overwhelmingly designed for acute treatment rather than long-term care. Hospitals
may address illness, but they are poorly equipped to support ageing. Policy responses exist,
but they operate in silos.


Private assisted living facilities and specialised care homes are expanding, but they remain
out of reach for most Indians. Meanwhile, publicly supported elder-care institutions are too
few to meet even a fraction of the demand. The result is an uncomfortable gap between
longevity and dignity. There is also a deeper societal cost. Loneliness among older adults is
no longer an exception. Social isolation contributes to mental distress, accelerates physical
decline, and increases dependence on emergency healthcare. These outcomes ultimately place
greater strain on public systems ~ the very systems that proactive investment could
strengthen rather than overwhelm. India’s ageing challenge should therefore be viewed not as
a welfare obligation alone, but as a matter of long-term economic planning. Countries that
age without preparing for care infrastructure often pay later through rising healthcare costs,
reduced workforce participation among caregivers, and widening inequality between those
who can afford support and those who cannot. What is needed is a shift in thinking.

questions.stimulus:
V. Union Home Minister Amit Shah has rightly stressed the need to make a distinction between
refugees and infiltrators. Although valid, the problem lies in the application of objective
parameters by those in power to draw distinctions. Even where proper policy and a legal
framework exist, issues may arise. Also at play is the level of official understanding. In India,
which is not a signatory to the 1951 UN Refugee Convention and the 1967 Protocol, there is
no comprehensive single law defining who a refugee is, leaving scope for arbitrary action. Till
the end of March 2025, apart from the Citizenship Act 1955 and the Passports Act 1967, three
laws (the Foreigners Act, 1946, the Registration of Foreigners Act, 1939 and the Passport
(Entry into India) Act, 1920) were applied to deal with foreign nationals, including refuge
seekers. From April, the Immigration and Foreigners Act replaced the three pre-Independence
laws and subsumed the Immigration (Carriers’ Liability) Act, 2000. While this streamlined the
legal framework, the absence of a refugee policy document has also led to different yardsticks
for the refugee community in India. While there was a rehabilitation policy in 2014 for about
63,000 Tibetan refugees, there is no such document for the nearly 90,000 Sri Lankan Tamils.
At the end of June 2023, the population of refugees or persons of concern in India was over
2.11 lakh (also counting those from Myanmar, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Africa and West Asia).
Any undocumented or overstaying refugee is regarded as an illegal migrant (Citizenship Act).
He can also be called an infiltrator. Thus, genuine and harmless refugees risk facing
harassment.
Even though the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 was aimed at providing citizenship to six
religious minorities belonging to Bangladesh, Pakistan and Afghanistan, it drew sharp criticism
as it discriminated on the lines of religion and left out sections of Muslims, and also Sri Lankan


Tamils and the Rohingya, both minorities in their countries. But in a notification last month,
undocumented or overstaying Tamil refugees, who have registered themselves with the
authorities, were granted exemption from penal provisions of the Immigration and Foreigners
Act, provided they took shelter in India on or before January 9, 2015. Other groups, too have
been covered. Still, there is no change in the recent trend of religion-based exclusions. There
is nothing fundamentally wrong with the approach of discreet humanitarian relief to refugees
in general but this has to be backed by consistent, rational and fair treatment for all.


SOURCE:https://www.thehindu.com/opinion/editorial/refugees-and-infiltrators-on-different-
yardsticks-for-indias-refugee-community/article70167639.ece

questions.stimulus:
V. Union Home Minister Amit Shah has rightly stressed the need to make a distinction between
refugees and infiltrators. Although valid, the problem lies in the application of objective
parameters by those in power to draw distinctions. Even where proper policy and a legal
framework exist, issues may arise. Also at play is the level of official understanding. In India,
which is not a signatory to the 1951 UN Refugee Convention and the 1967 Protocol, there is
no comprehensive single law defining who a refugee is, leaving scope for arbitrary action. Till
the end of March 2025, apart from the Citizenship Act 1955 and the Passports Act 1967, three
laws (the Foreigners Act, 1946, the Registration of Foreigners Act, 1939 and the Passport
(Entry into India) Act, 1920) were applied to deal with foreign nationals, including refuge
seekers. From April, the Immigration and Foreigners Act replaced the three pre-Independence
laws and subsumed the Immigration (Carriers’ Liability) Act, 2000. While this streamlined the
legal framework, the absence of a refugee policy document has also led to different yardsticks
for the refugee community in India. While there was a rehabilitation policy in 2014 for about
63,000 Tibetan refugees, there is no such document for the nearly 90,000 Sri Lankan Tamils.
At the end of June 2023, the population of refugees or persons of concern in India was over
2.11 lakh (also counting those from Myanmar, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Africa and West Asia).
Any undocumented or overstaying refugee is regarded as an illegal migrant (Citizenship Act).
He can also be called an infiltrator. Thus, genuine and harmless refugees risk facing
harassment.
Even though the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 was aimed at providing citizenship to six
religious minorities belonging to Bangladesh, Pakistan and Afghanistan, it drew sharp criticism
as it discriminated on the lines of religion and left out sections of Muslims, and also Sri Lankan


Tamils and the Rohingya, both minorities in their countries. But in a notification last month,
undocumented or overstaying Tamil refugees, who have registered themselves with the
authorities, were granted exemption from penal provisions of the Immigration and Foreigners
Act, provided they took shelter in India on or before January 9, 2015. Other groups, too have
been covered. Still, there is no change in the recent trend of religion-based exclusions. There
is nothing fundamentally wrong with the approach of discreet humanitarian relief to refugees
in general but this has to be backed by consistent, rational and fair treatment for all.

X. In a landmark judgment reinforcing the constitutional safeguards of judicial independence,
the Supreme Court of India struck down pivotal provisions of the Tribunal Reforms Act, 2021,
declaring them an unconstitutional encroachment by the executive into the judicial domain.
The Court held that the impugned provisions, by granting the Union government excessive
control over appointments, tenure, and service conditions of tribunal members, fundamentally
undermined the autonomy and impartiality of tribunals, thereby violating the separation of
powers—a cornerstone of the Constitution’s basic structure.
The Court meticulously invalidated several stipulations. It ruled the minimum age requirement
of 50 years for appointment as arbitrary, noting it unfairly excluded competent younger
advocates contrary to earlier rulings. The mandated four-year tenure for chairpersons and
members was struck down for fostering dependency and insecurity, with the Court reinstating
a minimum five-year term to ensure institutional continuity. Significantly, the provision


allowing the government a panel of two names per vacancy was nullified, with the directive
that the Search-cum-Selection Committee must recommend only one name to curtail executive
discretion. Equating tribunal members' service conditions with civil servants was also
invalidated, as it blurred the line between judicial and executive functions.

enacting provisions from a previously invalidated ordinance. It emphatically reiterated that
judicial review is part of the inviolable basic structure, and Parliament cannot nullify a binding
judgment merely by repackaging the same flawed law. To remedy systemic issues, the Court
mandated the establishment of a National Tribunal Commission within four months,
envisioning it as an independent oversight body to ensure transparency and uniformity in
tribunal administration. This decision serves as a potent reaffirmation of constitutional
supremacy, ensuring tribunals—as vital instruments of justice—remain insulated from
executive dominance to uphold fair and specialized adjudication.

questions.stimulus:
XI. Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the creation of a bailment imposes a fiduciary-like
relationship upon the bailee, the party receiving the goods, charging them with several specific
and non-delegable duties central to the arrangement’s integrity. The foremost obligation,
encapsulated in Section 151, is the duty to take reasonable care of the bailed goods. The statute
mandates a uniformly high objective standard: the bailee must exercise the same level of care
as “a man of ordinary prudence” would take of his own goods of similar value and nature. This
standard applies irrespective of whether the bailment is gratuitous or for reward, and failure to
meet it results in liability for any loss, damage, or destruction.
Crucially, the bailee’s right to use the goods is strictly circumscribed by the bailment’s purpose.
Section 154 imposes a duty not to make any unauthorized use of the goods. If the bailee uses
the goods in a manner inconsistent with the terms of the bailment, they become absolutely
liable for any loss or damage occurring during such use, even if caused by an accident or
through no apparent fault. This strict liability underscores the contractual sanctity of the
bailment’s agreed purpose. Furthermore, the bailee has a duty not to mix the bailor’s goods
with their own or a third party’s goods without the bailor’s consent (Sections 155-157).
Unauthorized mixing entitles the bailor to claim compensation for any expenses incurred in
separation or, if the goods cannot be separated, for the resultant loss in value.
Upon the accomplishment of the purpose or the expiry of the stipulated time, the bailee’s duty
under Section 160 is to return, or deliver according to the bailor’s directions, the goods without
waiting for any demand. This duty reinforces the temporary and specific-purpose nature of
bailment. Finally, recognizing the bailor’s enduring ownership, Section 163 obligates the bailee
to return or account for any accretion or benefits that may have accrued from the bailed goods
during the period of bailment, such as offspring from animals or profits earned. Collectively,
these statutory duties position the bailee as a responsible custodian, legally bound to protect


the bailor’s proprietary interest and ensure the goods’ safe return, thereby balancing the benefits
derived from possession with rigorous accountability.

relationship upon the bailee, the party receiving the goods, charging them with several specific
and non-delegable duties central to the arrangement’s integrity. The foremost obligation,

mandates a uniformly high objective standard: the bailee must exercise the same level of care
as “a man of ordinary prudence” would take of his own goods of similar value and nature. This
standard applies irrespective of whether the bailment is gratuitous or for reward, and failure to
meet it results in liability for any loss, damage, or destruction.

the goods in a manner inconsistent with the terms of the bailment, they become absolutely
liable for any loss or damage occurring during such use, even if caused by an accident or
through no apparent fault. This strict liability underscores the contractual sanctity of the
bailment’s agreed purpose. Furthermore, the bailee has a duty not to mix the bailor’s goods

separation or, if the goods cannot be separated, for the resultant loss in value.

XIII. The recent observation by a Supreme Court judge advocating for the decriminalisation of
defamation has reignited a critical constitutional debate in India, centred on the tension between
the fundamental right to reputation and the equally vital right to free speech. Presently,
defamation is governed under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (formerly IPC Sections 499
and 500), which prescribes criminal penalties, including imprisonment. This framework was
constitutionally validated by the Supreme Court in Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India
(2016), which held that protecting reputation is an integral part of the right to life under Article
21 and that criminal defamation constitutes a "reasonable restriction" on free speech under
Article 19(2).
However, growing judicial and academic discourse underscores the pressing need for reform.
Critics argue that criminal defamation is increasingly weaponised by powerful entities,
including political figures and corporations, to silence dissent, settle scores, and stifle
legitimate criticism through the threat of protracted and punitive criminal proceedings. This
creates a significant "chilling effect" on journalists, activists, and citizens, undermining
democratic discourse. Furthermore, the principle of proportionality is questioned, as
reputational harm is primarily a civil injury, and imprisonment is deemed an excessive remedy.
Many mature democracies, notably the United States, treat defamation solely as a civil wrong.
The path forward necessitates a balanced legislative recalibration. A pivotal measure would be
to decriminalise defamation in purely private disputes, restricting criminal liability to
statements concerning public interest that are made with proven actual malice. Concurrently,
civil remedies must be strengthened through fast-track courts, clear norms for compensation,
and promoting alternative dispute resolution to ensure efficient justice. To protect public
watchdogs, statutory safeguards for journalists and whistleblowers acting in good faith, along
with anti-SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation) legislation, are essential to
deter frivolous suits intended to harass. Ultimately, reforming India's defamation law is
imperative to foster a more robust culture of free expression while ensuring that reputation is
protected through civil means that are both effective and constitutionally proportionate.

the electoral cycles of the Lok Sabha and all State Legislative Assemblies, a practice prevalent
in India’s first two decades. The recent Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024, introduced
following the High-Level Committee (HLC) led by former President Ram Nath Kovind,
provides the legal architecture for this transition. The core legal mechanism involves inserting
Article 82A to empower the Election Commission to synchronize terms and declare a unified
schedule. Crucially, the bill proposes amendments to Articles 83 and 172, stipulating that
assemblies constituted after the foundational "appointed date" would serve only the remainder
of the Lok Sabha’s term, thereby creating a locked cycle for the future.

governance deficits caused by perpetual electioneering. Frequent elections perpetuate policy
paralysis due to the repeated imposition of the Model Code of Conduct, encourage short-term
populist fiscal measures, and place immense logistical strain on administrative and security
resources. Synchronization is posited to ensure political stability, enhance governance
continuity, and allow for more efficient long-term policy implementation by freeing
governments from constant electoral pressure.

curtailing or extending the constitutionally guaranteed five-year term of state assemblies for
mere synchronization raises serious concerns regarding federal autonomy and the basic
structure of the Constitution. It potentially undermines the direct mandate of state electorates

logistical hurdles are unprecedented, requiring massive augmentation of EVM/VVPAT
infrastructure and personnel for a single electoral event. The legal framework must also

XV. The doctrine of Absolute Liability is a seminal judicial innovation in Indian tort law,
established by the Supreme Court in the landmark 1987 case of M.C. Mehta vs. Union of India.
This ruling was delivered in the wake of the Oleum gas leak from a Delhi-based unit of Shriram
Food and Fertilizers, an incident that occurred shortly after the catastrophic Bhopal Gas
Tragedy. Recognizing the inadequacy of existing principles, the Court, under Justice Bhagwati,
consciously created a new rule distinct from the English rule of strict liability (Rylands v.
Fletcher). The Court reasoned that the old doctrine, with its numerous exceptions, was
insufficient to address the grave risks posed by modern, profit-driven hazardous industries. The
underlying rationale is that an enterprise which engages in inherently dangerous activity for
economic gain must bear the social responsibility for any harm caused, treating compensation
as a necessary cost of its business operations.
This new principle is critically distinguished from strict liability on two key grounds. First,
while strict liability requires the "escape" of a dangerous thing from the defendant's land,
absolute liability applies even if the harm occurs within the enterprise's premises, such as to
workers or visitors. Second, and most significantly, strict liability admits several exceptions
like Act of God, plaintiff's fault, or act of a third party. Absolute liability admits no exceptions
whatsoever, making the enterprise liable regardless of any supervening circumstance or fault.
As a corollary, the Court integrated the "Polluter Pays" principle, mandating that the offending
enterprise must bear the cost of remediating the damaged environment in addition to
compensating human victims.
In scope and application, the doctrine covers industries like chemical plants, fertilizer units,
nuclear installations, and hazardous waste facilities. The types of harm encompass death,
personal injury, property damage, and environmental degradation. A defining characteristic is
that no traditional defences are admissible; the defendant cannot plead that it took all
reasonable care, that the harm was caused by an Act of God or sabotage, or that the victim was
contributorily negligent. This makes absolute liability the most stringent standard, placing an
unwavering duty of safety on hazardous enterprises.

questions.stimulus:
XIX. Creative writing used to be a human prerogative: do it well, do it badly, but either way
endorse the consensus that to write about human experience was worth the candle and the
coffee. Here was an essential human act, so much so that poetry formed a critical part of the
computer pioneer Alan Turing’s original test: to determine whether an unseen respondent to a
series of questions was human or a mechanical imposter. The Turing Test is often simplified to
denote a single crossing point between two territories, human and machine. Pass the test, and
artificial intelligence can stroll on over to our side of the line. Take a look around. Decide what
to do with us. But, first, it has to pass.
In the paper ‘Computing Machinery and Intelligence’ (1950), published in the journal Mind,
Turing set out his objective: ‘to consider the question, “Can machines think?”’ In true human
fashion, he immediately re-phrases the question, at some length, and eventually arrives at the
‘imitation game’, modelled on a drawing-room entertainment from before the internet, before
television. The original game he has in mind involves a guesser in the hotseat who poses
questions to a man (X) and a woman (Y), who are out of sight and hearing in a separate room.
The guesser has to determine from their written answers which is the man and which is the
woman. X tries to mislead, and wins if the guesser is wrong; Y wins if the guesser is right. Try
it, it’s fun.
In this context, the first question posed in Turing’s proposed test is less surprising than at first
it seems: ‘Will X please tell me the length of his or her hair?’ Next, Turing asks, equally
politely: ‘Please write me a sonnet on the subject of the Forth Bridge.’ Two questions in, and
the contested boundary between human and machine thinking is already looking for answers
in literature, in art. Turing’s 1950s version of X – the participant aiming to mislead – replies:
‘Count me out on this one. I never could write poetry.’ To imagine this answer, in the second
phase of his game, Turing’s complicated brain is playing the role of a machine playing X,
hidden from sight and typing its answers, pretending to be a man (who previously played the
game pretending to be a woman). I know, but if the test were easy an air-fryer could pass it.

XIX. Creative writing used to be a human prerogative: do it well, do it badly, but either way
endorse the consensus that to write about human experience was worth the candle and the
coffee. Here was an essential human act, so much so that poetry formed a critical part of the
computer pioneer Alan Turing’s original test: to determine whether an unseen respondent to a
series of questions was human or a mechanical imposter. The Turing Test is often simplified to
denote a single crossing point between two territories, human and machine. Pass the test, and
artificial intelligence can stroll on over to our side of the line. Take a look around. Decide what
to do with us. But, first, it has to pass.
In the paper ‘Computing Machinery and Intelligence’ (1950), published in the journal Mind,
Turing set out his objective: ‘to consider the question, “Can machines think?”’ In true human
fashion, he immediately re-phrases the question, at some length, and eventually arrives at the
‘imitation game’, modelled on a drawing-room entertainment from before the internet, before
television. The original game he has in mind involves a guesser in the hotseat who poses
questions to a man (X) and a woman (Y), who are out of sight and hearing in a separate room.
The guesser has to determine from their written answers which is the man and which is the
woman. X tries to mislead, and wins if the guesser is wrong; Y wins if the guesser is right. Try
it, it’s fun.

it seems: ‘Will X please tell me the length of his or her hair?’ Next, Turing asks, equally
politely: ‘Please write me a sonnet on the subject of the Forth Bridge.’ Two questions in, and
the contested boundary between human and machine thinking is already looking for answers
in literature, in art. Turing’s 1950s version of X – the participant aiming to mislead – replies:
‘Count me out on this one. I never could write poetry.’ To imagine this answer, in the second
phase of his game, Turing’s complicated brain is playing the role of a machine playing X,
hidden from sight and typing its answers, pretending to be a man (who previously played the
game pretending to be a woman). I know, but if the test were easy an air-fryer could pass it.
